<response>\boxed{- Data sources and coverage: Kantar blends filings, POS panels, card‑spend panels, and surveys. Gaps for private or non‑reporting companies require estimates, which can over‑ or understate sales and shift rankings. 
- Definition of “retail sales”: Results depend on whether Kantar includes services (fees, memberships), fuel, autos, restaurants, pharmacies, wholesale/B2B, and returns/discounts. Different inclusion rules change who qualifies and their sales totals.
- Marketplace vs first‑party: Counting third‑party GMV (e.g., marketplace sales) versus only first‑party/net sales can dramatically change the size of e‑commerce players.
- Omnichannel allocation: How buy‑online‑pick‑up, delivery, and ship‑from‑store sales are attributed (store vs online) affects category and retailer comparisons.
- Company consolidation rules: Whether sales are rolled up to the parent across banners and franchises, and whether franchisee gross sales are counted, can raise or lower a chain’s total.
- Geography and currency/inflation adjustments: If Kantar limits to U.S. sales, converts currencies, and inflation‑adjusts, the choices and timing of these adjustments affect comparability.
- Time period alignment: Retailers have different fiscal years. Kantar’s normalization (or lack of it) can capture or miss peaks, promotions, or pandemic base effects, altering ranks.
- M&A and store changes: How Kantar treats acquisitions, divestitures, and closures within the period can inflate or depress a retailer’s reported sales.
- Modeling and sampling error: Imputation, panel bias, and rounding introduce uncertainty, especially for niche sectors or rapidly growing DTC brands.

Net effect: The “50 largest” is an informed estimate that depends on Kantar’s definitions, coverage, and modeling choices. Different, reasonable methodologies could yield a different order—or even a different set—of top retailers.}</response>

detections.label: The University of Notre Dame will confer 3,147 degrees during Commencement Weekend Saturday
Degrees will be conferred on 2,025 undergraduate students at Notre Dame's 174th University
Commencement Ceremony on Sunday. Pulitzer Prize-winning columnist for the Wall Street Journal,
speechwriter for President Ronald Reagan and author of five New York Times best-sellers Peg.gy.
Noonan will be the principal speaker and recipient of an honorary degree. Norman C. Francis, civil
rights leader and longtime president of Xavier University in Louisiana, will receive the 2o19 Laetare
(lay-TAH-ray)Medal, the oldest and most prestigious honor given to American Catholics.
Sofia Carozza, a neuroscience and behavior major with a supplemental major in theology from South
Bend, Indiana, will deliver the valedictory address. Salutatorian Annelise Gill-Wiehl, an
environmental engineering major from St. Louis, Missouri, will deliver the invocation.
In addition to Noonan, five others will receive honorary degrees. They are Carol Corrigan, associate
justice of the California Supreme Court; James Poterba, the Mitsui Professor of Economics at the
Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Ignacio Sánchez, longtime faculty member in the School of
Medicine and president of Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile; Esther Takeuchi, distinguished
professor in the departments of materials science and chemical engineering, and chemistry at Stony
Brook University; and john Affleck-Graves, executive vice president and chair of the department of
finance who is retiring from his administration role on June 30.
On Saturday, 513 students will receive master's and doctoral degrees at the Graduate School
Commencement Ceremony, along with 387 master's degree students at the Mendoza College of
Business Ceremony and 222 at the Law School Ceremony.
Some notable Commencement weekend events are:
• The ROTC Commissioning Ceremony, 9 a.m. Saturday, Leighton Concert Hall, DeBartolo
.The Graduate School Commencement Ceremony, 10 a.m. Saturday, Compton Family Ice Arena.
· The Mendoza College of Business Graduate Business Ceremony, 10 a.m. Saturday, Purcell Pavilion,
. The Law School Ceremony, 12:30 p.m. Saturday, Hesburgh Library Reflecting Pool.
.The Service Send-Off Ceremony, 1 p.m. Saturday, Leighton Concert Hall, DeBartolo Performing
Commencement Mass, 5 p.m. Saturday,Purcell Pavilion,Joyce Center.
• The undergraduate college and department diploma ceremonies beginning at 2 p.m. Sunday
A complete schedule of events is available from the Commencement website.
The academic processional will begin at 9:30 a.m. Sunday. All attendees must have a ticket for
admission. Guests can enter the stadium beginning at 8 a.m. through Gate A on the northeast side
and Gate B on the southeast side.
Many common items will be prohibited from entering the stadium during Commencement. For a
complete list of prohibited items,visit the Commencement website.
Contact: Sue Ryan, director of media relations, 574-631-7916, sue.ryan@nd.edu
Originally published by Sue Ryan at news.nd.edu on May 13, 2019.

detections.label: The University of Notre Dame will confer 3,147 degrees during Commencement Weekend Saturday
Degrees will be conferred on 2,025 undergraduate students at Notre Dame's 174th University
Commencement Ceremony on Sunday. Pulitzer Prize-winning columnist for the Wall Street Journal,
speechwriter for President Ronald Reagan and author of five New York Times best-sellers Peg.gy.
Noonan will be the principal speaker and recipient of an honorary degree. Norman C. Francis, civil
rights leader and longtime president of Xavier University in Louisiana, will receive the 2o19 Laetare
(lay-TAH-ray)Medal, the oldest and most prestigious honor given to American Catholics.
Sofia Carozza, a neuroscience and behavior major with a supplemental major in theology from South
Bend, Indiana, will deliver the valedictory address. Salutatorian Annelise Gill-Wiehl, an
environmental engineering major from St. Louis, Missouri, will deliver the invocation.
In addition to Noonan, five others will receive honorary degrees. They are Carol Corrigan, associate
justice of the California Supreme Court; James Poterba, the Mitsui Professor of Economics at the
Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Ignacio Sánchez, longtime faculty member in the School of
Medicine and president of Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile; Esther Takeuchi, distinguished
professor in the departments of materials science and chemical engineering, and chemistry at Stony
Brook University; and john Affleck-Graves, executive vice president and chair of the department of
finance who is retiring from his administration role on June 30.
On Saturday, 513 students will receive master's and doctoral degrees at the Graduate School
Commencement Ceremony, along with 387 master's degree students at the Mendoza College of
Business Ceremony and 222 at the Law School Ceremony.
Some notable Commencement weekend events are:
• The ROTC Commissioning Ceremony, 9 a.m. Saturday, Leighton Concert Hall, DeBartolo
.The Graduate School Commencement Ceremony, 10 a.m. Saturday, Compton Family Ice Arena.
· The Mendoza College of Business Graduate Business Ceremony, 10 a.m. Saturday, Purcell Pavilion,
. The Law School Ceremony, 12:30 p.m. Saturday, Hesburgh Library Reflecting Pool.
.The Service Send-Off Ceremony, 1 p.m. Saturday, Leighton Concert Hall, DeBartolo Performing
Commencement Mass, 5 p.m. Saturday,Purcell Pavilion,Joyce Center.
• The undergraduate college and department diploma ceremonies beginning at 2 p.m. Sunday
A complete schedule of events is available from the Commencement website.
The academic processional will begin at 9:30 a.m. Sunday. All attendees must have a ticket for
admission. Guests can enter the stadium beginning at 8 a.m. through Gate A on the northeast side
and Gate B on the southeast side.
Many common items will be prohibited from entering the stadium during Commencement. For a
complete list of prohibited items,visit the Commencement website.
Contact: Sue Ryan, director of media relations, 574-631-7916, sue.ryan@nd.edu
Originally published by Sue Ryan at news.nd.edu on May 13, 2019.

detections.label: The University of Notre Dame will confer 3,147 degrees during Commencement Weekend Saturday
Degrees will be conferred on 2,025 undergraduate students at Notre Dame's 174th University
Commencement Ceremony on Sunday. Pulitzer Prize-winning columnist for the Wall Street Journal,
speechwriter for President Ronald Reagan and author of five New York Times best-sellers Peg.gy.
Noonan will be the principal speaker and recipient of an honorary degree. Norman C. Francis, civil
rights leader and longtime president of Xavier University in Louisiana, will receive the 2o19 Laetare
(lay-TAH-ray)Medal, the oldest and most prestigious honor given to American Catholics.
Sofia Carozza, a neuroscience and behavior major with a supplemental major in theology from South
Bend, Indiana, will deliver the valedictory address. Salutatorian Annelise Gill-Wiehl, an
environmental engineering major from St. Louis, Missouri, will deliver the invocation.
In addition to Noonan, five others will receive honorary degrees. They are Carol Corrigan, associate
justice of the California Supreme Court; James Poterba, the Mitsui Professor of Economics at the
Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Ignacio Sánchez, longtime faculty member in the School of
Medicine and president of Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile; Esther Takeuchi, distinguished
professor in the departments of materials science and chemical engineering, and chemistry at Stony
Brook University; and john Affleck-Graves, executive vice president and chair of the department of
finance who is retiring from his administration role on June 30.
On Saturday, 513 students will receive master's and doctoral degrees at the Graduate School
Commencement Ceremony, along with 387 master's degree students at the Mendoza College of
Business Ceremony and 222 at the Law School Ceremony.
Some notable Commencement weekend events are:
• The ROTC Commissioning Ceremony, 9 a.m. Saturday, Leighton Concert Hall, DeBartolo
.The Graduate School Commencement Ceremony, 10 a.m. Saturday, Compton Family Ice Arena.
· The Mendoza College of Business Graduate Business Ceremony, 10 a.m. Saturday, Purcell Pavilion,
. The Law School Ceremony, 12:30 p.m. Saturday, Hesburgh Library Reflecting Pool.
.The Service Send-Off Ceremony, 1 p.m. Saturday, Leighton Concert Hall, DeBartolo Performing
Commencement Mass, 5 p.m. Saturday,Purcell Pavilion,Joyce Center.
• The undergraduate college and department diploma ceremonies beginning at 2 p.m. Sunday
A complete schedule of events is available from the Commencement website.
The academic processional will begin at 9:30 a.m. Sunday. All attendees must have a ticket for
admission. Guests can enter the stadium beginning at 8 a.m. through Gate A on the northeast side
and Gate B on the southeast side.
Many common items will be prohibited from entering the stadium during Commencement. For a
complete list of prohibited items,visit the Commencement website.

The football adventures of Peter Miles
Gefle Idrottsförening, or GIF, were formed in December 1882 as Gefle SK
although the current name was adopted only months later. Gefle itself is the
ancient spelling of Gavle a port town around 1l0 miles north of Stockholm.
The port and town thrived on exports of copper and iron and remains a busy
hub for sea transportation. The town is renowned internationally for the
Gavle goat, a huge straw goat that is erected and burnt every yuletide.
As with many clubs in Sweden the GlF club was originally a multi sports club
that then created a football offshoot.In the case of Gefle,football was
introduced to the town by an English accountant called Robert Carrick.
Carrick would manage the club until 1907. During his tenure the club gained
early success in the short lived Rosenska Pokalen winning the first three
tournaments defeating AlK twice and also Djurgardens IF in the finals. At the
time the club refused to participate in the Svenska Masterskapet which was
a cup tournament held to decide the best team in all of Sweden with the final
alternating between Gothenburg and Stockholm. This meant probably the
best side in the east of the country at the time never tested itself against
Gothenburg's Örgryte IS who were the dominant side in the early years of
Since those early successes Gefle have mainly been a second and third tier
club with two short spells in the Allsvenskan in the 1930's and 1980's. The
1950's were a dark period for the club and having sunk to the fourth tier the
board actively discussed folding the club altogether.In 1979 the club briefly

Mediterranean-style cooking. This, of course, pushed me towards using
more olive oil. Butter went from a staring role in most of my meals to
an supporting and indulgent role for certain recipes. And as one would
the latest food trends even when
expect my rate of grocery store purchases of butter dropped
time is in precious short supply.
dramatically. More recently though I noticed a gradual increase in
recipes calling for butter. Maybe it has been because of our increasing
dalliance into new types of ethnic recipes which call for for wonderfully
rich ingredients like butter and ghee. It could be due in part to a
certain amount of consumer disillusionment with the previous claims of
the"heart-healthy" virtues of margarine.I think it also has something
to do with just the natural circle of life in all trends (every trend seems
to come back into style eventually).

current while being mindful of what staple ingredients your target

If you thought one of the biggest oil spills in history would automatically propel strong legislation to cap carbon
emissions and avert a climate crisis, think again.
Democratic Senate leaders beat back a conservative attempt to kneecap the EPA's ability to regulate greenhouse gas
emissions, but not without six Dems defecting. Only 53 Senators backed the EPA, and even some of those did so
And I say"only 53," even though that's a majority, because any climate bill will need 60 votes, period. The Senate voted
overwhelmingly last year to prevent climate legislation from being eligible for a simple majority vote under Senate
That level of support for regulating carbon pollution is pretty much the same before the Gulf gusher as after. Certainly no
Senator announced a change in position in the aftermath of the disaster.

challenging and requiring frustrating compromises -- remain the same.

states (Louisiana) or wanna-be offshore oil producing states (Virginia). Still more come from energy-intensive
And you stil need to find a few Republicans to get to 60, the path to which according to the utterly maddening Sen.
Lindsey Graham, lies in compromises for more nuclear power and, as you may have heard, offshore drilling. Such a deal
has had tacit support from major environmental groups but is now harder to seal in the wake of the BP blowout.
Grist's David Roberts, with whom I almost always agree, argued yesterday that the Murkowski vote in and of itself is
meaningless and the climate bill's prospects partly rest on "the level of public anger on the oil spill." But that anger is at
its peak today. And people are not making a direct connection between the oil in the water and the carbon in the
atmosphere, or at least, skittish politicians are assuming they are not.
So, where does that leave us? Is any climate bill possible in this environment?
The momentum presently is going the wrong way, away from the Kerry-Lieberman American Power Act (already chock
full of tough compromises) towards an clean energy investment bill with a weaker carbon cap, or no cap at all.

If you thought one of the biggest oil spills in history would automatically propel strong legislation to cap carbon
emissions and avert a climate crisis, think again.
Democratic Senate leaders beat back a conservative attempt to kneecap the EPA's ability to regulate greenhouse gas
emissions, but not without six Dems defecting. Only 53 Senators backed the EPA, and even some of those did so
And I say"only 53," even though that's a majority, because any climate bill will need 60 votes, period. The Senate voted
overwhelmingly last year to prevent climate legislation from being eligible for a simple majority vote under Senate
That level of support for regulating carbon pollution is pretty much the same before the Gulf gusher as after. Certainly no
Senator announced a change in position in the aftermath of the disaster.
Why? Because the complex political dynamics - which make passing transformational energy legislation extremely
challenging and requiring frustrating compromises -- remain the same.
18 Democratic Senators hail from the top coal-producing states. Key right-leaning Senators come from oil producing
states (Louisiana) or wanna-be offshore oil producing states (Virginia). Still more come from energy-intensive
And you stil need to find a few Republicans to get to 60, the path to which according to the utterly maddening Sen.
Lindsey Graham, lies in compromises for more nuclear power and, as you may have heard, offshore drilling. Such a deal
has had tacit support from major environmental groups but is now harder to seal in the wake of the BP blowout.
Grist's David Roberts, with whom I almost always agree, argued yesterday that the Murkowski vote in and of itself is
meaningless and the climate bill's prospects partly rest on "the level of public anger on the oil spill." But that anger is at
its peak today. And people are not making a direct connection between the oil in the water and the carbon in the
atmosphere, or at least, skittish politicians are assuming they are not.
So, where does that leave us? Is any climate bill possible in this environment?
The momentum presently is going the wrong way, away from the Kerry-Lieberman American Power Act (already chock
full of tough compromises) towards an clean energy investment bill with a weaker carbon cap, or no cap at all.

results.ground_truth_answer:
Direct factors:

* At least 60 votes are required to pass a bill

Indirect factors:

* Level of public anger on environmental issues/assessment of the politicians over public sentiment on environmental issues
* People don't make a direct connection between the oil in the water and the carbon in the atmosphere
* Eighteen Democratic Senators hail from the top coal-producing states, affecting their biases


Key right-leaning Senators come from oil-producing states (Louisiana) or offshore oil-producing states (Virginia). Still, more come from energy-intensive manufacturing states or agribusiness states. These stats indicate the Senators' reluctance toward the passing of the climate bill, thus making it a big factor for the passing of the climate bill.

the United States of America, including section 202 of the Revised Statutes (22
U.S.C.2656)and section 3161 oftitle 5, United States Code, it is hereby
Section 1. Establishment. There is esta blished within the Department of State,
in accordance with section 3161 of title 5, United States Code, a temporary
organization to be known as the Pakistan and Afghanistan Sup port Office
Sec. 2. Purpose of the Temporary Organization. The purpose ofthe PASO
shall be to perform the specific project of supporting executive departments
and agencies in strengthening the governments in Afghanistan and Pakistan,
enhancing the capacity ofthose governments to resist extremists, and
maintaining an effective U.S. diplomatic presence in both countries.
Sec. 3. Functions of the Temporary Organization. In carrying out the purpose
set forth in section 2, the PASO shall:
(a) support executive departments and agencies in efforts to enhance civilian
control and stable constitutional government in Pakistan, to promote a more
capable,accountable, and effective government in Afghanistan that serves the
Afghan people and eventually can function, especially regarding internal
security, with limited international support, and to stimulate an economy that
will provide licit opportunity for the people of Pakistan and Afghanistan;
(b) assume the functions assigned to the Afghanistan Support Office (ASO) as
ofthe date of this order; and
(c) perform such other functionsrelated to the specific project set forth in
section 2 as the Secretary of State(Secretary) may assign.
Sec. 4. Personnel and Administration. The PASO shall be headed by a Director
appointed by the Secretary. The PASO shall be based in Washington, D.C.
Pakistan, and Afghanistan. The Secretary shall transfer from the ASO to the

over the last decade they have become friends of ours and fed us meals beyond belief.

partly because he (as do l) want fish like Bluefin tuna to be around to eat in the next few years.
There's a lot ofinfo at www.seafoodwatch.org about what's safe and what's not.
His restaurant is Mashiko (his sustainable message is here)
I was up there last week and my friends and I spent about 6 hours there eating and drinking.
He says business is hurting because things like eel are off the menu. Well every sushi restaurant in the
US gets their eel pre cooked and pre marinated in the sugar sauce and in plastic shrink wrap.It's not
really that good, its sweet but it's stupidly popular in the US. He's found that catfish makes a suitable
substitute and with food that is masked by sauce people wouldn't know the difference if he didn't tell him.
I could go on for hours (and he could go on further) about the nitrogen used on maguro (tuna) to keep it at
White tuna is not tuna,it's escolar.
Chilean Sea Bass is neither from Chile nor is it a Sea Bass.
There's no rules in fish sales and it's all marketing and Hajime has been no BS since day one.
Anyway..he's doing somethingreally good, the food is still phenomenal and  thought you might want to

Corwin"this Thurs 10/8 at6pm (I Think onFood Network).

in the autumn.Food sustains us, and it should be a source of great pleasure as well.
2.The Environment: We are stewards of this Earth, from the top of Mount Kilimanjaro to the bottom of the
sea.It's our duty and our honor to care for it.

The internal organization and dynamics of eukaryotic cells is largely determined by the framework of cytoskeletal
elements and molecular motors that transport organelles and macromolecular complexes to specif c destinations in the
cell. Long range transport is generally mediated by microtubule-based motors, and short range transport and capture
by the actin-based motors, myosins. The myosin-V family ofmolecular motors is evolutionarily highly conserved
between animals, plants and fungi, and defects in vertebrate myosin-Vs can cause disease. Many different organelles are
transported by myosin-Vs, but how they recognize specific cargo, transport and release it at its destination is poorly
understood.To address these questions,the researchers use budding yeast where the essential myosin-V,encoded by
Myo2,transports secretory vesicles for growth as its major cargo, butalso transports peroxisomes, compartments of
the secretory pathway, and the vacuole for segregation during the cell cycle, and microtubule ends for nuclear
orientation prior to mitosis.These transport events are all mediated by organelle-specif c receptors, many of which are
known. Here the researchers explore three fundamental aspects of the Myo2 secretory vesicle delivery cycle. In the frst
aim, they use quantitative live-cell imagining to quantify the number of motors per secretory vesicle and establish how
this is determined,and the kinetics of the delivery cycle and how this is integrated with tethering and fusion of the
vesicles at their destination. They also explore mechanisms forrecycling and regulation of Myo2. In the second aim,
they use genetic and live cell imaging methods to explore the function of two proteins, Mmr1 and Smy1,that bind the
tail of Myo2 and seem to play a role in its delivery cycle. In the third aim, they first propose to exploit genetic and
biochemical approaches to extend their studies on the receptor by which Myo2 identifes and binds secretory vesicles.
They also explore the relationship between binding sites on the Myo2 cargo-binding tail by identifying specifc
mutations that compromise the interactions with individual receptors, and also exploring how binding to one receptor
affects binding to another.Finally, they propose to set up an in vitro assay toreconstitute the binding of Myo2 to
secretory vesicles based on the genetic, biochemical and cell biological information collected in the earlier aims. Overall,
this study will provide unprecedented insights into the delivery cycle of Myo2, which will be of broad relevance due to

The internal organization and dynamics of eukaryotic cells is largely determined by the framework of cytoskeletal
elements and molecular motors that transport organelles and macromolecular complexes to specif c destinations in the
cell. Long range transport is generally mediated by microtubule-based motors, and short range transport and capture
by the actin-based motors, myosins. The myosin-V family ofmolecular motors is evolutionarily highly conserved
between animals, plants and fungi, and defects in vertebrate myosin-Vs can cause disease. Many different organelles are
transported by myosin-Vs, but how they recognize specific cargo, transport and release it at its destination is poorly
understood.To address these questions,the researchers use budding yeast where the essential myosin-V,encoded by
Myo2,transports secretory vesicles for growth as its major cargo, butalso transports peroxisomes, compartments of
the secretory pathway, and the vacuole for segregation during the cell cycle, and microtubule ends for nuclear
orientation prior to mitosis.These transport events are all mediated by organelle-specif c receptors, many of which are
known. Here the researchers explore three fundamental aspects of the Myo2 secretory vesicle delivery cycle. In the frst
aim, they use quantitative live-cell imagining to quantify the number of motors per secretory vesicle and establish how
this is determined,and the kinetics of the delivery cycle and how this is integrated with tethering and fusion of the
vesicles at their destination. They also explore mechanisms forrecycling and regulation of Myo2. In the second aim,
they use genetic and live cell imaging methods to explore the function of two proteins, Mmr1 and Smy1,that bind the
tail of Myo2 and seem to play a role in its delivery cycle. In the third aim, they first propose to exploit genetic and
biochemical approaches to extend their studies on the receptor by which Myo2 identifes and binds secretory vesicles.
They also explore the relationship between binding sites on the Myo2 cargo-binding tail by identifying specifc
mutations that compromise the interactions with individual receptors, and also exploring how binding to one receptor
affects binding to another.Finally, they propose to set up an in vitro assay toreconstitute the binding of Myo2 to

The internal organization and dynamics of eukaryotic cells is largely determined by the framework of cytoskeletal
elements and molecular motors that transport organelles and macromolecular complexes to specif c destinations in the
cell. Long range transport is generally mediated by microtubule-based motors, and short range transport and capture
by the actin-based motors, myosins. The myosin-V family ofmolecular motors is evolutionarily highly conserved
between animals, plants and fungi, and defects in vertebrate myosin-Vs can cause disease. Many different organelles are
transported by myosin-Vs, but how they recognize specific cargo, transport and release it at its destination is poorly
understood.To address these questions,the researchers use budding yeast where the essential myosin-V,encoded by
Myo2,transports secretory vesicles for growth as its major cargo, butalso transports peroxisomes, compartments of
the secretory pathway, and the vacuole for segregation during the cell cycle, and microtubule ends for nuclear
orientation prior to mitosis.These transport events are all mediated by organelle-specif c receptors, many of which are
known. Here the researchers explore three fundamental aspects of the Myo2 secretory vesicle delivery cycle. In the frst
aim, they use quantitative live-cell imagining to quantify the number of motors per secretory vesicle and establish how
this is determined,and the kinetics of the delivery cycle and how this is integrated with tethering and fusion of the
vesicles at their destination. They also explore mechanisms forrecycling and regulation of Myo2. In the second aim,
they use genetic and live cell imaging methods to explore the function of two proteins, Mmr1 and Smy1,that bind the
tail of Myo2 and seem to play a role in its delivery cycle. In the third aim, they first propose to exploit genetic and
biochemical approaches to extend their studies on the receptor by which Myo2 identifes and binds secretory vesicles.
They also explore the relationship between binding sites on the Myo2 cargo-binding tail by identifying specifc
mutations that compromise the interactions with individual receptors, and also exploring how binding to one receptor
affects binding to another.Finally, they propose to set up an in vitro assay toreconstitute the binding of Myo2 to
secretory vesicles based on the genetic, biochemical and cell biological information collected in the earlier aims. Overall,

detections.label: When her American grandparents visited last
month, they gave Nora a homework
assignment to be completed by the time they
visit again in August: to learn to smile in
baby talk. She has taken the assignment very
seriously and has been practicing ever since.
The first time I ever saw her truly smile, combined with a
not-yet-laughter cooing noise, was in our hotel room in
Madrid two weekends ago. I had her in my arms and was
recounting the exciting morning of planes, trains, and
automobiles. Her face lit up and I saw the most beautiful
sight I think I've ever seen. Or at least I did for a few
seconds before my smile raised my cheekbones up over my
eyes and, tears welled up, and everything went blurry.
Paralyzed by joy,the storytelling stopped, and eventually
we eased back down off of cloud nine. Marga reports the
same teary-eyed emotional paralysis and can't recall
anything for those few heavenly moments either.
Naturally we've done little else than seek this high ever
since. Nora, like a manipulative drug dealer with her
junkies, has only given us small samples of joy ever since,
but has yet to repeat the full-on high of nine days ago. What
follows is an attempt I made yesterday to capture an image
What you're about to see will make you smile. If you've just
had reconstructive facial surgery, or are in a dentist's chair,
please navigate away now to something sad.

Two tips for people who need to install new flooring in their
If you need to replace your home's flooring (including both the uppermost layer and the flooring system underneath it), here are a few tips
that you may want to keep in mind.
Buy the best floor trusses you can afford
You don't necessarily need to spend a small fortune on every single part of your new flooring system; for example,if there are rooms in your
home that are not exposed to a lot of foot traffic, then it should be perfectly fine to use low-cost carpeting or linoleum in these areas of your
However,you should not scrimp when it comes to the floor trusses.'Economy'brand floor trusses will be far less robust than their more
expensive counterparts. Cheap floor trusses often lack the pesticides, fungicides and waterproofing chemicals that are found in high-end
trusses.As such, if you opt for low-cost trusses and some termites take up residence in your property,or if one of the water pipes bursts open
and floods your home, the condition of the trusses will deteriorate rapidly.
This deterioration could affect the ability of the trusses to withstand the weight of the objects that are placed on the floor.This could then
result in the floorboards bowing or becoming distorted.As such, itis best to purchase the highest-quality floor trusses you can afford.
Think about your lifestyle when choosing between carpeting and hard floors
When choosing between carpeting and hard floor materials (like tile, timber or linoleum,for example), it's important not to base your choice
solely on what youfeelwill look best, but also on what will suit your lifestyle.
For example, if you have pets that are not yet house trained or if you have young children who frequently spill their drinks and food on the
floors, then it might not be a great idea to opt for carpeting, as this type of flooring is highly absorbent. As a result, it will be difficult to
properly clean up any accidents or spillages, and keep the flooring smelling fresh. In this situation, hard floors would be a far better choice,as
any liquids that land on them can be removed quickly and easily, and there is very little chance of the floors becoming stained or malodorous.
Conversely, if you or your family members have health conditions that could increase your risk of falling (such as vertigo, for example) or if
you have health conditions that mean that a fall could have serious repercussions (for instance, if you have osteoporosis and are very likely to
suffer a bone fracture if you fall), then it would be best to opt for a deep-pile carpet rather than hard flooring.This is because tiles, lino and
varnished timber are all very slippery and, as such, could increase your chances of falling.Additionally, because they are very hard, you are
much more likely to sustain a serious injury if you do end up falling. In this scenario, carpeting that provides plenty of traction and which is
quite soft and cushioned would be a far wiser choice.
To learn more, contact a company like Simon Home Timber & Hardware.
2023© Keeping Your Carpets and Floors Clean

results.ground_truth_answer:
Based on information in the paragraphs under the "Pay for Essays at Lowest Rate", it is mentioned that the customer can redeem a 15% discount on their first order by writing the code "PRO-PAPERS15", after their first order the user gets a lifetime discount of 5% until after their 5th order it increases to 10% until their 15th order where every order gets a 15% lifetime discount, so now if we calculate the total discount achieved from all the orders:

* **First Order:** 15%
* **Orders 2–5:** 4×5%=20%
* **Orders 6–15:** 10×10%=100%
* **Order 16:** 15%

**Total -** 15% + 20% + 100% + 15% = **150% total discounts from purchases.**
So the user can achieve around **150%** discount from the original prices of the 16 orders

results.ground_truth_answer: Information about the number of posts on a monthly basis and in the year 2009 is given at the top of the right sidebar. February contributed 7.29% (14/192 \* 100%), and August, September, and November each contributed 6.77% (13/192 \* 100%). results.ground_truth_answer: Meal planning using Melissa’s two cookbooks, *Well Fed* and *Well Fed 2*, ensures both variety and adherence to the Whole30 diet's clean eating guidelines by providing clear, Whole30-approved recipes. These cookbooks offer a structure for meal planning, making it easier to know what to eat and when. Purchasing essential grocery items upfront, such as spices, oils, and nut flours, helps simplify the process, reduces costs, and eliminates the need for frequent grocery trips. A single, well-planned shopping trip can cover the entire 30-day period, saving time, energy, and travel expenses. Together, these strategies make the Whole30 diet more sustainable and increase the likelihood of successfully completing the 30-day reset.

- Manchester United defense (4-4-2): De Gea; Rafael (RB), Ferdinand (RCB), Evans (LCB), Evra (LB). Wide midfielders ahead of them are Valencia (right) and Giggs (left), with Cleverley central.

Manchester United defensive strengths vs West Brom attack
- Centre-back experience and reading of play: Ferdinand (RCB) + Evans (LCB) give composure and positioning to manage Lukaku’s hold-up play and to step in front when he receives to feet.
- Aerial coverage: Evans and Ferdinand are strong in the air, helpful against Lukaku’s aerial threat and crosses from Brunt/Odemwingie.

- Space behind adventurous fullbacks: With Valencia and Giggs as wide mids, both fullbacks (Rafael, Evra) are encouraged to push. Brunt (left) and Odemwingie (right) can counter into the spaces left behind, especially if Cleverley/Giggs don’t track.

- If United keep their fullbacks’ balance and get protection from Valencia/Giggs/Cleverley, their aerial strength and experience should cope with Lukaku and limit crosses—advantage United.
- If West Brom can win turnovers and attack quickly into the channels behind Rafael/Evra or exploit set pieces, they can stress United’s back line—danger comes from transitions and dead balls.

<response>\boxed{Assessment grounded in the page:
- What changed per the page: Tidal “has … includ[ed] a free tier” and, more importantly, launched consumer profiles with proper playlist sharing. Playlists can be made public, are discoverable via search, and are sharable by link. Profiles are live across Android, iOS, desktop, and web, and existing saved content is preserved when creating a profile.

Likely impact on user engagement:
- Lower barrier to entry: The free tier lets price-sensitive users try Tidal without commitment, increasing sign-ups and first-play events.
- Higher activation: Profiles and easy playlist sharing give new users something to do immediately (create/curate/share), speeding time-to-first-value.
- Stronger retention: Public profiles and saved-content migration reduce switching friction and loss aversion; users who invest in playlists are more likely to return.
- More time in-app: Social discovery (searchable/public playlists) encourages browsing, following, and longer listening sessions.
- Network effects: As users share links externally, recipients are pulled into Tidal’s app/site, creating organic re-engagement loops.

Likely impact on market growth:
- Closes competitive gap: Free tier + social/playlist features align Tidal with mainstream rivals, improving appeal in regions where paid adoption lags.
- Viral distribution: Link-based sharing turns every playlist into a lightweight acquisition channel (creator/influencer-driven growth).
- Cross-platform reach: Simultaneous Android/iOS/desktop/web availability maximizes addressable audience and reduces friction in work/commute/home contexts.
- Upsell pathway: Free users who build libraries and social ties are prime candidates for conversion to paid (for ad-free, offline, higher-quality audio).

Key metrics to watch:
- Top of funnel: New accounts, cost per acquisition, share-driven installs/visits, K-factor (invites per user × conversion).
- Engagement: DAU/MAU, sessions/user, time spent listening, playlists created/shared, follow actions, search-driven playlist views.
- Retention and monetization: Free-to-paid conversion rate, churn by cohort, ARPU, ad monetization RPM vs. streaming royalty costs.

Risks and mitigations:
- Margin pressure/cannibalization: Free listening incurs royalties; mitigate via ad load tuning, feature gating, and targeted upsell.
- Content moderation/privacy: Public profiles require tools for reporting, curation controls, and clear privacy defaults.
- Fragmented experience: Ensure seamless migration from “My Selection” and strong onboarding so users understand profiles/sharing.

Bottom line:
- The free-tier strategy, paired with profiles and frictionless playlist sharing across all platforms, is likely to materially lift user engagement (creation, discovery, listening time) and drive market growth through viral acquisition and improved competitive parity—provided Tidal manages free-tier economics and converts engaged cohorts to paid.} </response>

\boxed{Assessment grounded in the page:
- What changed per the page: Tidal “has … includ[ed] a free tier” and, more importantly, launched consumer profiles with proper playlist sharing. Playlists can be made public, are discoverable via search, and are sharable by link. Profiles are live across Android, iOS, desktop, and web, and existing saved content is preserved when creating a profile.

Likely impact on user engagement:
- Lower barrier to entry: The free tier lets price-sensitive users try Tidal without commitment, increasing sign-ups and first-play events.
- Higher activation: Profiles and easy playlist sharing give new users something to do immediately (create/curate/share), speeding time-to-first-value.
- Stronger retention: Public profiles and saved-content migration reduce switching friction and loss aversion; users who invest in playlists are more likely to return.
- More time in-app: Social discovery (searchable/public playlists) encourages browsing, following, and longer listening sessions.
- Network effects: As users share links externally, recipients are pulled into Tidal’s app/site, creating organic re-engagement loops.

Likely impact on market growth:
- Closes competitive gap: Free tier + social/playlist features align Tidal with mainstream rivals, improving appeal in regions where paid adoption lags.
- Viral distribution: Link-based sharing turns every playlist into a lightweight acquisition channel (creator/influencer-driven growth).
- Cross-platform reach: Simultaneous Android/iOS/desktop/web availability maximizes addressable audience and reduces friction in work/commute/home contexts.
- Upsell pathway: Free users who build libraries and social ties are prime candidates for conversion to paid (for ad-free, offline, higher-quality audio).

Key metrics to watch:
- Top of funnel: New accounts, cost per acquisition, share-driven installs/visits, K-factor (invites per user × conversion).
- Engagement: DAU/MAU, sessions/user, time spent listening, playlists created/shared, follow actions, search-driven playlist views.
- Retention and monetization: Free-to-paid conversion rate, churn by cohort, ARPU, ad monetization RPM vs. streaming royalty costs.

Risks and mitigations:
- Margin pressure/cannibalization: Free listening incurs royalties; mitigate via ad load tuning, feature gating, and targeted upsell.
- Content moderation/privacy: Public profiles require tools for reporting, curation controls, and clear privacy defaults.
- Fragmented experience: Ensure seamless migration from “My Selection” and strong onboarding so users understand profiles/sharing.

Bottom line:
- The free-tier strategy, paired with profiles and frictionless playlist sharing across all platforms, is likely to materially lift user engagement (creation, discovery, listening time) and drive market growth through viral acquisition and improved competitive parity—provided Tidal manages free-tier economics and converts engaged cohorts to paid.}

The historical weather data serves to emphasize the importance of timing and soil conditions for successful planting in such a fluctuating climate.

results.ground_truth_answer:
The table in the middle of the screenshot, titled "Toronto Land Transfer Tax Changes 2017" lists all the tax rates according to the tax brackets applicable. According to that table, LTT for a $2,500,000 property after March 1, 2017:

* Bracket 1 ($0 to $55,000 at 0.5%): 55,000 × 0.005 = $275
* Bracket 2 ($55,001 to $250,000 at 1.0%): 195,000 × 0.01 = $1,950
* Bracket 3 ($250,001 to $400,000 at 1.5%): 150,000 × 0.015 = $2,250
* Bracket 4 ($400,001 to $2,000,000 at 2.0%): 1,600,000 × 0.02 = $32,000
* Bracket 5 (Over $2,000,000 at 2.5%): 500,000 × 0.025 = $12,500

Total LTT: $275 + $1,950 + $2,250 + $32,000 + $12,500 = $48,975. A client has to pay $48,975 Land Transfer Tas(LTT) for a property purchased after March 1, 2017.

results.ground_truth_answer:
The table titled "Toronto Land Transfer Tax Changes 2017" in the middle of the screenshot lists all the tax rates according to applicable tax brackets. The only tax rate change for a Non-Residential Property is in the tax bracket range (400,000 to 2,000,000) according to the text below the table which states, "\* This text range is applicable for Residential properties only. Non-residential properties in this range are taxed at a rate of 2.5%". The asteroid (\*) is present only in the range (400,000 to 2,000,000). From this information, the tax rate for the range (400,000 to 2,000,000) is 2.0% for Residential properties and 2.5% for Non-residential properties. According to that table, the LTT calculation for a Non-Residential Property ($3,000,000) is:

* 0.5% on $55,000 = $275
* 1.0% on $195,000 ($250,000 - $55,000) = $1,950
* 1.5% on $150,000 ($400,000 - $250,000) = $2,250
* 2.5% on $1,600,000 ($2,000,000 - $400,000) = $40,000
* 2.5% on $1,000,000 ($3,000,000 - $2,000,000) = $25,000
* Total MLTT = $69,475

Percentage Contribution by Bracket:

* 0.5% on $55,000: (275 ÷ 69,475) × 100 = 0.40%
* 1.0% on $195,000: (1,950 ÷ 69,475) × 100 = 2.81%
* 1.5% on $150,000: (2,250 ÷ 69,475) × 100 = 3.24%
* 2.5% on $1,600,000: (40,000 ÷ 69,475) × 100 = 57.57%
* 2.5% on $1,000,000: (25,000 ÷ 69,475) × 100 = 35.98%

Residential Property ($3,000,000):
LTT Calculation:

* 0.5% on $55,000 = $275
* 1.0% on $195,000 = $1,950
* 1.5% on $150,000 = $2,250
* 2.0% on $1,600,000 ($2,000,000 - $400,000) = $32,000
* 2.5% on $1,000,000 ($3,000,000 - $2,000,000) = $25,000
* Total MLTT = $61,475

Percentage Contribution by Bracket:

* 0.5% on $55,000: (275 ÷ 61,475) × 100 = 0.45%
* 1.0% on $195,000: (1,950 ÷ 61,475) × 100 = 3.17%
* 1.5% on $150,000: (2,250 ÷ 61,475) × 100 = 3.66%
* 2.0% on $1,600,000: (32,000 ÷ 61,475) × 100 = 52.06%
* 2.5% on $1,000,000: (25,000 ÷ 61,475) × 100 = 40.66%

For non-residential properties, the 2.5% applied to the portion between $400,000 and $2,000,000 contributes 57.57% of the total LTT, and the 2.5% applied to the portion over $2,000,000 contributes 35.98%. This clearly shows the heavy weighting of the tax burden on the portions of the property value above $400,000. For residential properties, the 2.0% applied to the portion between $400,000 and $2,000,000 contributes 52.06%, and the 2.5% applied to the portion over $2,000,000 contributes 40.66%. The burden is more evenly distributed between these two higher brackets compared to the non-residential case. This demonstrates that non-residential LTT at this price point is structured to place a significantly larger proportion of the tax burden on the value above $400,000, making it more progressive than the residential LTT at this price point.

results.final_answer:
\boxed{- Key differences:
  - Separate documents: A will and a trust are distinct legal instruments used in a unified estate plan and can sometimes conflict.
  - Timing: A will takes effect at death; a revocable (living) trust becomes operative during the grantor’s lifetime.
  - Control/Priority: If there’s a discrepancy regarding assets titled to the trust or naming the trust as beneficiary (e.g., life insurance), the revocable trust controls over the will.
  - Legal nature and probate: A trust is a separate legal entity; when the grantor dies, assets in the revocable trust are not part of the decedent’s probate process.

- Why a grantor might choose a revocable trust:
  - To have an instrument that operates during life and is changeable at any time while the grantor is alive.
  - To ensure the trust’s terms govern assets titled to or benefiting the trust, even if a will says otherwise.
  - To keep trust-held assets out of probate, streamlining post‑death administration.}

How these sections drive engagement
- Clear topical segmentation: Four distinct blocks let users quickly self-select content that matches their interests (human-interest, policy, gender equity, economy), reducing cognitive load and bounce.
- Visual card layout: Each section surfaces 2–3 story cards with thumbnails and short headlines, enabling scanning and encouraging click-through from multiple entry points.
- Recency and utility cues: Headlines like “Roundup of Egypt’s press headlines” signal timely coverage; utility content (e.g., city growth, economic reforms) promises actionable insight.
- Breadth of perspectives: Pairing Politics with Business and Women’s Issues broadens representation and attracts communities that might not visit for general news alone.
- Placement in a two-row grid: Above-the-fold visibility for Life/Politics and near-fold visibility for Women’s Issues/Business encourages continuing scroll and additional clicks.
- Social extension: The “facebook comments” area below fosters discussion, providing social proof and return visits.

Strategies to attract diverse demographics through these categories
- Life (general audience, younger readers, families)
  - Use explainer mini-guides, how-tos, and culture/lifestyle features; emphasize photos, short videos, quizzes, and local service journalism.
  - Distribute on Instagram/TikTok; push notifications for city updates and events.
- Politics (civically engaged readers, activists, students)
  - Add timelines, fact-check boxes, “what changed” summaries, and weekly roundups; host live blogs and Q&As.
  - Promote on X/Facebook and through push alerts for breaking policy news; create a civics newsletter.
- Women’s Issues (women and allies, NGOs, educators)
  - Feature solutions journalism, resources (hotlines, legal guides), profiles, and data on equity; offer safe-commenting and moderated forums.
  - Partner with advocacy groups; run thematic series and Instagram Reels highlighting voices and success stories.
- Business (professionals, entrepreneurs, students)
  - Provide market snapshots, explainers, and data visualizations; publish brief “morning update” and “week-in-charts.”
  - Distribute via LinkedIn/WhatsApp channels; host webinars with economists/entrepreneurs.

Cross-cutting tactics
- Personalization: Recommend across sections (e.g., from Politics to Business explainers; from Life to Women’s Issues features).
- SEO and structure: Clear category hubs, keyword-rich summaries, schema for news articles, and internal linking among the four sections.
- Accessibility and language: Offer Arabic/English toggles, readable typography, captions on videos, and alt text on images.
- Community features: Polls, comment prompts, and UGC callouts tailored to each section.
- Measurement: Track CTR per section, scroll depth, time-on-page, return frequency, and newsletter signups to iterate content mix.

Together, this categorical layout captures varied interests, increases the number of clickable surfaces, and supports targeted distribution and personalization that broaden audience reach and deepen engagement.}
